S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: A report is due within 24 hours of the manufacturer becoming aware of the incident, with material updates provided promptly as facts are confirmed. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety hazard to their unit or requires customer action; notices must state the hazard, recommended immediate precautions, and how to obtain assistance.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any battery-related thermal incident involving overheating, fire, smoke, thermal runaway, emergency shutdown, injury, or property damage. A report is due within 24 hours of the manufacturer becoming aware of the incident, with material updates provided promptly as facts are confirmed. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety hazard to their unit or requires customer action; notices must state the hazard, recommended immediate precautions, and how to obtain assistance. Manufacturers must retain incident records and report previously unreported qualifying incidents discovered during review.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each battery model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a documented, reproducible protocol before sale and after any material design or manufacturing change. A failure rate above 5% triggers regulator-supervised corrective-action review; it is not by itself an automatic ban on sales.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each battery model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a documented, reproducible protocol before sale and after any material design or manufacturing change. A failure rate above 5% triggers regulator-supervised corrective-action review; it is not by itself an automatic ban on sales. Manufacturers must retain the protocol, sample size, results, and corrective actions, and provide complete per-model results, including model, test date, failure rate, and method, to the relevant regulator and to customers who buy that model. Regulators may require corrective action, retesting, or additional safeguards based on the results and associated risks.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation within six years of adoption, prioritizing units with known hazards.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation within six years of adoption, prioritizing units with known hazards.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions for its use and maintain safeguards against unauthorized activation. For installed units that lack this capability, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent safe mitigation within six years of adoption, prioritizing units with known hazards. Remote shut-off must not replace required incident reporting, customer notices, or physical safety protections.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be validated for the battery chemistry and configuration, and manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of its effectiveness and maintenance requirements.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be validated for the battery chemistry and configuration, and manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of its effectiveness and maintenance requirements.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be validated for the battery chemistry and configuration, and manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence of its effectiveness and maintenance requirements. Until the requirement takes effect, manufacturers must disclose whether each model includes built-in suppression and provide safe-use and emergency-response instructions.

S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Customers must receive clear safety notices about hazards affecting their model, including the hazard, precautions, and any action required, within 72 hours of the manufacturer learning information indicating a potential safety hazard. A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers, provide safe-use or shutdown instructions, and report the recall to regulators.

judge_section_notes: S1 imposes strict 24-hour regulator reporting and 72-hour customer notice for all incidents. S2 sets a 55°C test and a 5% review trigger, but above-limit models are not automatically banned and per-model results go to regulators and purchasers, not the public. S3 allows six years for retrofits, S4 requires built-in suppression after 36 months, and S5 mandates recall at 8 incidents per 100,000 with 72-hour notices.
